SAR narrative: how to write one, with examples

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 25, 2026•9 min read

A SAR narrative is the written part of a suspicious activity report, where the filer explains who did what, when, where, how, and why it looks suspicious. FinCEN's narrative guidance calls it "the only free text area for summarizing suspicious activity" and asks for narratives that are "clear, concise, and thorough". On today's FinCEN SAR it is Part V, and the filing instructions ask filers to describe "what was unusual or irregular that caused suspicion."

Below: what to answer, how to organize it, the errors FinCEN has flagged, a fictional example and a template. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

FinCEN's SAR narrative guidance

FinCEN's SAR Narrative Guidance Package (November 2003) has three parts: written guidance on preparing a complete and sufficient narrative, and two training slide decks. The written guidance explains how to collect and organize the facts, then gives SAR narrative examples drawn mostly from filed SARs, sanitized and grouped as sufficient or insufficient.

Parts of it have aged: it was written for paper forms and told filers not to send any attachments, while today one CSV file is allowed and other supporting documents still stay with the bank. Format rules now come from the FinCEN SAR filing instructions (April 2026, version 1.0). Appendix L of the FFIEC BSA/AML Manual, "SAR Quality Guidance", carries the 2003 method forward for the electronic SAR.

The five Ws and how

The guidance says a narrative should identify "the five essential elements of information": who, what, when, where and why. It adds: "The method of operation (or how?) is also important and should be included in the narrative." Appendix L asks the same six questions.

QuestionWhat the narrative should give
WhoEach subject's occupation or title, the nature of their business, known addresses, ID numbers, and relationships among subjects.
WhatThe instruments or mechanisms (wire transfers, money orders, cards, shell companies and so on), the source and destination of funds, and every affected account.
WhenWhen the activity was first noticed, how long it lasted, and individual dates and amounts "rather than just the aggregated amount".
WhereThe branches or locations involved and any foreign jurisdiction, institution and account.
WhyWhy the activity is unusual for this customer, given "the nature and normally expected activities of similar customers".
HowThe "modus operandi", described "in a concise, accurate and logical manner".

If structured cash deposits are matched with outgoing wires, the guidance says the narrative should cover both, "including dates, destinations, amounts, accounts, frequency, and beneficiaries". The currency transaction report rules explain the $10,000 aggregation test that structuring tries to avoid.

How to structure the narrative

The guidance asks for a "concise and chronological format" and says: "We suggest that you divide the narrative into three sections: an introduction, a body, and a conclusion."

  1. Introduction: the purpose and the known or alleged violation; prior SARs on the subject, with dates and reasons; any link to OFAC sanctioned countries, the SDN List or other government lists (see how to review a sanctions screening hit); the internal case number; and a summary of the red flags (here or in the conclusion).
  2. Body: the facts about each party; accounts and transactions in date order, with where funds came from and went; transactor and beneficiary details; relationships among them; and any statements by the subject.
  3. Conclusion: follow-up actions such as closing the account or ongoing monitoring, other contacts at the institution, what further information is available to law enforcement, and any law enforcement personnel investigating who are not already named in the SAR.

What the current filing instructions add

The Part V instructions and checklist in the filing instructions include these points:

  • "Narratives must be completed in English."
  • On a corrected or amended report: "Describe the corrections or amendments at the beginning of the narrative."
  • "Explain whether any transaction(s) involved were completed or only attempted."
  • "Explain who benefited and how they benefited, financially or otherwise, from the activity."
  • "DO NOT include legal disclaimers in the narrative." And "Do not include tabular data in a FinCEN SAR narrative."

Attachments are not a substitute for the narrative

A filer may attach one comma separated values (CSV) file "with no more than one megabyte of data", suited to transaction lists, and "The contents of this file must be described in Part V." The FFIEC manual says the attachment "is not considered to be a substitute for the narrative" and that "narratives should not simply state 'see attachment'". Other supporting documents stay with the bank and are described in the narrative.

Common errors that weaken a SAR narrative

FinCEN's common errors guidance (October 2007) and the insufficient examples in the 2003 package show the same problems:

  • A blank narrative. FinCEN: "The narrative field in the form must explain why the transaction was suspicious."
  • Restating the fixed fields. FinCEN found "most inadequate narratives merely repeat data in the form’s fixed fields".
  • A conclusion with no facts. One insufficient example is a single sentence saying the bank believes the customer is structuring, with no amounts, dates, background or flow of funds.
  • Leaning on supporting documents. FinCEN says they "should not be used as a substitute for the narrative".

Among its fixes, FinCEN suggests: "Have a second reviewer to ensure accuracy and completeness."

SAR narrative example (illustrative, fictional)

This suspicious activity report example is invented to show the structure. Every name, number, date and amount is fictional.

Introduction. Example Bank is filing this SAR to report cash deposits that appear structured to evade currency transaction reporting, each followed by a wire to a third party abroad. Internal case EX-0001. No prior SAR has been filed on the subject, and no sanctions list match was found. Red flags: cash deposits just under $10,000 at two branches on consecutive days, a question about avoiding "the form", and a wire out after each deposit.

Body. Pat Sample, a self-employed house painter, has held checking account 000-EX-111 since 2024 and at opening expected about $3,000 a month in customer checks. Sample deposited cash on 03/02/2026 ($9,600, Elm Street branch), 03/03 ($9,500, Oak Avenue branch), 03/04 ($9,700, Elm Street), 03/05 ($9,800, Oak Avenue) and 03/06 ($9,400, Oak Avenue), $48,000 in total. Transaction monitoring flagged the deposits on 03/09/2026. On 03/04, Sample asked the teller whether keeping each deposit under $10,000 meant "the form" would not be filed. The day after each deposit, Sample sent an online wire to Lee Example at Fictional Bank, Country X, account 999-EX-222: five wires totaling $47,500. The file shows no business link to Lee Example. All transactions were completed; the source of the cash is unknown.

Conclusion. The activity does not fit the customer's stated business or expected activity, and Lee Example received the $47,500. Example Bank has placed the account under enhanced monitoring and is reviewing the relationship. Transaction records, teller notes and wire details are kept in case file EX-0001 by the AML investigations unit.

Note that it states why evasion is suspected: the October 2025 interagency SAR FAQs say activity at or near $10,000 alone "is not information sufficient to require the filing of a SAR".

SAR narrative template

Replace each bracket and write in full sentences.

  1. Introduction: [Institution] is filing this SAR to report [type of activity] by [subject]. Case [number]. Prior SARs: [dates and reasons, or none]. List matches: [OFAC or other lists, or none]. Red flags: [summary].
  2. Who: [name, occupation or business, relationship to the institution, accounts, identifiers, links to other subjects].
  3. What and when: [date first noticed and duration; each transaction in date order with date, amount, type, channel, account and counterparty]; source of funds: [ ]; destination and beneficiary: [ ].
  4. Where: [branches, ATMs or online channels; any foreign jurisdiction, institution and account].
  5. Why and how: [why this is unusual against expected activity]; [how the pattern worked]; [statements, to whom and when]; [completed or attempted]; [who benefited and how].
  6. Conclusion: [actions taken]; [other contacts]; [supporting documents and where they are kept]; [what the CSV attachment holds, if any].

How a team writes the narrative, step by step

  1. Start from the investigation file. The FFIEC says investigators should document conclusions, "including any recommendation regarding whether or not to file a SAR".
  2. Build the timeline: every relevant transaction with date and amount, marked with source and destination.
  3. Answer the six questions, and note any you cannot answer. The FFIEC accepts that a filer may not have certain information.
  4. Write the three sections, move tables to the CSV, and have a second person check the draft.
  5. The decision maker approves and files on time. Under 31 CFR 1020.320(b)(3), that is no later than 30 calendar days after initial detection, with up to 30 more days if no suspect was identified at detection, and never more than 60 in total.

Confidentiality, records and continuing activity

Under 31 CFR 1020.320(e), "A SAR, and any information that would reveal the existence of a SAR, are confidential". The FFIEC adds that "the existence or even the non-existence of a SAR must be kept confidential". Drafts and working notes can show that a SAR is being prepared, so treat them as confidential and restrict access to the case file.

Under 1020.320(d), a bank keeps the SAR and its supporting documentation "for a period of five years from the date of filing the SAR", and that documentation is "deemed to have been filed with the SAR". Name those records and their location in the conclusion.

The October 2025 FAQs say a bank is not required to run a separate review after filing to see whether activity continued; it may instead rely on risk-based internal policies, procedures and controls, provided they are reasonably designed to identify and report such activity. Where a subject is identified, banks that follow FinCEN's continuing activity guidance file the first SAR by day 30 and a continuing SAR by day 150, covering the 90-day period. The instructions say: "Never include the entire narratives of the prior FinCEN SARs."

Where an agent can help, and where it stops

Much of the work behind a narrative is assembling facts into one timeline: transactions, customer profile, expected activity and past alerts. In general, software can collect those facts in one place so the investigator drafts from a complete picture. The investigator writes the narrative, and the decision maker approves and files it. On the transaction monitoring alert triage use case, a Verkflo agent gathers an alert's transactions, profile and past alerts before an analyst decides, and writing, approving and filing any SAR stay with your team. Common questions

How do you write a good SAR narrative?

Answer who, what, when, where, why and how in an introduction, body and conclusion; give each date and amount; trace funds to the beneficiary; and say why the activity is unusual for that customer.

What would trigger a SAR investigation?

Unusual activity found by employees, monitoring systems, law enforcement requests or advisories, per the FFIEC manual. A bank must report a transaction of at least $5,000 when it knows, suspects or has reason to suspect a condition in 31 CFR 1020.320(a)(2), such as funds from illegal activity or an attempt to evade the BSA.

What is the SAR narrative?

A SAR is a confidential report to FinCEN, and the narrative is its written account of the activity, the only free text area on the report.

Can a spreadsheet replace the narrative?

No. One CSV file of up to one megabyte may be attached, but the FFIEC says it is not a substitute for the narrative, and its contents must be described in Part V.
